The [SHA-256 Hash Generator](/sha256-hash-generator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Generate a SHA-256 hash of any text — free, instant and private. Enter your text to hash and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Generate the SHA-256 hash of any text. SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function: it turns any input into a fixed 64-character hexadecimal fingerprint, and the same input always produces the same hash, while even a one-character change produces a completely different one. It is used to verify file integrity, store passwords safely (with a salt), and sign data. The hashing runs in your browser with the Web Crypto API — your text is never uploaded or stored.

## How to use the SHA-256 Hash Generator

Start by typing or pasting your text to hash. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Type or paste the text you want to hash.
2. The SHA-256 hash appears instantly, in hexadecimal and in Base64.
3. Copy the hash with the copy button.

## Formula

SHA-256 processes the input in 512-bit blocks through 64 rounds of mixing, and outputs a 256-bit digest shown as 64 hexadecimal characters. It is a one-way function: you cannot recover the input from the hash.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [SHA-256 Hash Generator](/sha256-hash-generator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The SHA-256 hash of “Hello, world!” is 315f5bdb76d078c43b8ac0064e4a0164612b1fce77c869345bfc94c75894edd3. Change one letter and the hash changes completely. Try the same figures in the [SHA-256 Hash Generator](/sha256-hash-generator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

Change one input at a time and watch how the result responds — that tells you more than any description. ## What a hash is for

A hash is a fingerprint: it lets you check that data has not changed without storing the data itself. Download a file, hash it, and compare with the hash the publisher lists — if they match, the file is intact. Password systems store hashes (with a unique salt per user) instead of passwords, so a leaked database does not expose the passwords. Git uses SHA-1 and now SHA-256 to identify every commit.

## Why SHA-256 is trusted

SHA-256 is part of the SHA-2 family standardised by NIST and used across the internet — in TLS certificates, Bitcoin, and software signing. No practical attack can reverse it or find two different inputs with the same hash. Short or common inputs are still vulnerable to guessing (an attacker can hash a dictionary and compare), which is why passwords need a salt and a slow hash function such as bcrypt or Argon2 rather than plain SHA-256.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The same input always gives the same hash — use that to verify downloads.
- Never use plain SHA-256 to store passwords; use bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 with a salt.
- Hashing is one-way: you cannot turn a hash back into the original text.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is SHA-256?

A cryptographic hash function that turns any input into a fixed 256-bit (64 hex character) fingerprint. It is deterministic, one-way, and a tiny change in the input produces a completely different hash. Try it with your own numbers in the [SHA-256 Hash Generator](/sha256-hash-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Is SHA-256 secure?

Yes, for integrity checking and signatures. For password storage it is not enough on its own — use a slow, salted hash such as bcrypt or Argon2 instead, because plain SHA-256 is too fast for an attacker to brute-force. Try it with your own numbers in the [SHA-256 Hash Generator](/sha256-hash-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
